note: Mark's summary of Jesus' message is compact and urgent: {mk 1:15 Πεπλήρωται ὁ καιρὸς} (“the time is fulfilled”). Matthew changes Mark's “kingdom of **God**” to {mt 4:17 ἡ βασιλεία τῶν οὐρανῶν} (“kingdom of the **heavens**”), as he does almost everywhere, a reverent Jewish way of avoiding God's name. He also adds an Isaiah quotation about {mt 4:15 Γαλιλαία τῶν ἐθνῶν} (“Galilee of the Gentiles”).

Luke places this rejection at the very start of Jesus' ministry (on the traditional reading, an earlier, separate visit) and expands it into a programmatic sermon on Isaiah 61, ending in an attempt to kill him. Matthew follows Mark closely but changes two awkward details. Mark's Jesus is {mk 6:3 ὁ τέκτων} (“the carpenter”), Matthew's {mt 13:55 ὁ τοῦ τέκτονος υἱός} (“the carpenter's son”). And Mark's {mk 6:5 οὐκ ἐδύνατο} (“he **could** not”) becomes {mt 13:58 οὐκ ἐποίησεν} (“he **did** not”).

Matthew copies Mark's call story almost word for word, including the memorable {mt 4:19 ποιήσω ὑμᾶς ἁλιεῖς ἀνθρώπων} (“I will make you fishers of people”). Luke replaces it with a miraculous catch of fish and a different verb, {lk 5:10 ἀνθρώπους ἔσῃ ζωγρῶν} (*zōgrōn*, “catching alive”). John tells a strikingly similar catch, but after the resurrection, with exactly {jn 21:11 ἑκατὸν πεντήκοντα τριῶν} (153) fish. Traditional harmonies take Luke's catch as a later, fuller call of men who had already met Jesus, and John's as a deliberate echo of it.

Mark and Luke share a 26-word verbatim run here. Matthew skips the exorcism but borrows one sentence from it to close the Sermon on the Mount: {mt 7:29 ἦν γὰρ διδάσκων αὐτοὺς ὡς ἐξουσίαν ἔχων} (“for he taught them as one having authority”), almost exactly Mark's words. The demon's cry {mk 1:24 οἶδά σε τίς εἶ ὁ ἅγιος τοῦ θεοῦ} (“I know who you are, the Holy One of God”) begins Mark's pattern of demons who recognize Jesus before people do.

A small but telling change: in Mark, Jesus {mk 1:31 ἤγειρεν αὐτὴν κρατήσας τῆς χειρός} (“raised her, taking her hand”). Matthew has him simply touch her, and then she raises herself: {mt 8:15 ἠγέρθη} (“she was raised”). The verb *egeirō* is the same one used for resurrection. Matthew also has her serve {mt 8:15 αὐτῷ} (“him”, Jesus) instead of Mark's “them”.

Matthew turns Mark's summary into a scripture fulfillment, citing Isaiah 53:4: {mt 8:17 Αὐτὸς τὰς ἀσθενείας ἡμῶν ἔλαβεν} (“he took our weaknesses”). Mark ends instead with secrecy: Jesus would not let the demons speak {mk 1:34 ὅτι ᾔδεισαν αὐτόν} (“because they knew him”). Luke makes explicit what they knew, {lk 4:41 τὸν χριστὸν αὐτὸν εἶναι} (“that he was the Christ”).

Mark has Jesus rise {mk 1:35 πρωῒ ἔννυχα λίαν} (“very early, still at night”) to pray alone, a detail Matthew omits. Mark's “that is why I **came out**” ({mk 1:38 εἰς τοῦτο γὰρ ἐξῆλθον}) could mean “came out from the town” or “came out from God”. Luke settles the ambiguity with {lk 4:43 ἐπὶ τοῦτο ἀπεστάλην} (“for this I was **sent**”) and adds his favorite verb of divine necessity, *dei* (“I must”).

Matthew and Luke both add {mt 8:2 Κύριε} (“Lord”) to the leper's plea, a word Mark doesn't have here (a minor agreement), and both drop Mark's report of Jesus' emotion (see the Discovery). Mark ends with an ironic reversal: the healed man spreads the news so widely that Jesus {mk 1:45 μηκέτι αὐτὸν δύνασθαι φανερῶς εἰς πόλιν εἰσελθεῖν} (“could no longer openly enter a town”), becoming an outcast himself.

The central saying, from “which is easier” to “to forgive sins”, is nearly identical in all three, including the awkward broken sentence where Jesus turns mid-speech to the paralytic. Copying would preserve such an anacoluthon, but independent oral retelling would probably smooth it out. Matthew and Luke agree against Mark on small details, such as {mt 9:2 ἐπὶ κλίνης} (“on a bed”) and {lk 5:25 ἀπῆλθεν εἰς τὸν οἶκον αὐτοῦ} (“went off to his house”).

Mark and Luke call the tax collector {mk 2:14 Λευὶν τὸν τοῦ Ἁλφαίου} (“Levi son of Alphaeus”), but Matthew renames him {mt 9:9 Μαθθαῖον λεγόμενον} (“named Matthew”). This is one reason later tradition linked the apostle Matthew with this Gospel. The traditional reading is that Levi and Matthew are one man with two names, like Simon and Peter. Matthew also adds Hosea 6:6, {mt 9:13 Ἔλεος θέλω καὶ οὐ θυσίαν} (“I desire mercy, not sacrifice”), which he will quote again in 12:7.

Matthew changes Mark's “can the wedding guests **fast**” to {mt 9:15 πενθεῖν} (“**mourn**”), making the connection to grief and the coming death explicit. Luke adds a closing line found only in his Gospel that cuts against the parable's point: {lk 5:39 Ὁ παλαιὸς χρηστός ἐστιν} (“the old is good”). It may be a wry comment on why people resist the new.

Mark says David ate the sacred bread {mk 2:26 ἐπὶ Ἀβιαθὰρ ἀρχιερέως} (“when Abiathar was high priest”), but according to 1 Samuel 21 the priest was Abiathar's father, Ahimelech. Defenders of Mark note that *epi Abiathar* can mean “in the passage about Abiathar”, the way Jews cited scripture sections, or that Abiathar, later the famous high priest, was present at the time. **Both** Matthew and Luke drop the phrase. Both also omit Mark's bold {mk 2:27 Τὸ σάββατον διὰ τὸν ἄνθρωπον ἐγένετο} (“the Sabbath was made for humankind”). Matthew instead adds two arguments of his own, including {mt 12:6 τοῦ ἱεροῦ μεῖζόν ἐστιν ὧδε} (“something greater than the temple is here”).

Mark gives Jesus a rare emotional moment: he looks around {mk 3:5 μετ ὀργῆς συλλυπούμενος} (“with anger, grieved”) at their hardness of heart. Luke keeps the look, {lk 6:10 περιβλεψάμενος πάντας αὐτοὺς}, but drops the anger; Matthew drops the whole sentence. This fits a recurring pattern, in which the later Gospels soften Mark's portrayal of Jesus' emotions.

Mark's summary ends with unclean spirits shouting {mk 3:11 Σὺ εἶ ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ} (“you are the Son of God”) and Jesus silencing them. Matthew replaces this with his longest fulfillment quotation, Isaiah 42:1–4, which presents Jesus as the gentle Servant: {mt 12:18 Ἰδοὺ ὁ παῖς μου ὃν ᾑρέτισα} (“here is my servant whom I have chosen”). The shared wording here is low.

Only Mark gives the Aramaic nickname {mk 3:17 Βοανηργές ὅ ἐστιν Υἱοὶ Βροντῆς} (“Boanerges, that is, Sons of Thunder”) for James and John. Matthew calls Simon {mt 10:2 πρῶτος} (“first”), a word that matches his special interest in Peter. Luke has Jesus pray all night before choosing them, and his list differs: {lk 6:16 Ἰούδαν Ἰακώβου} (“Judas son of James”) appears where Mark and Matthew have Thaddaeus.
